content: A thorough examination for the presence of a tick is necessary to rule out tick paralysis, which typically manifests as an ascending pattern of muscle paralysis. Heavy metal poisoning can present with symptoms involving the gastrointestinal tract, alopecia (hair loss), mental disturbances such as irritability, difficulty concentrating, and somnolence, as well as peripheral neuropathy. Organophosphate toxicity is characterized by a cholinergic syndrome. Botulism should be considered as a probable diagnosis even in the absence of a history of consuming home-canned foods. Classic symptoms of botulism include bilateral cranial nerve palsies and a descending pattern of muscle weakness. The incubation period for botulism is typically 18 to 36 hours. Therefore, obtaining a detailed dietary history for this time frame is crucial. If botulism is suspected, the local or state health department must be contacted immediately. In cases of botulism intoxication, electromyography (EMG) of the affected muscles, performed with rapid repetitive stimulation at 20–50 Hz, usually demonstrates a potentiated response in muscle action potentials. In contrast, Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and myasthenia gravis show flat and decremental responses, respectively, with rapid repetitive stimulation. The administration of Tensilon (edrophonium) can confirm the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis by demonstrating improved muscle strength following injection of the compound. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein levels are normal in botulism but are almost always elevated in GBS, except in the early stages of the illness. A CT scan of the head, with and without contrast, can help rule out significant cerebrovascular accidents or encephalitis. An MRI may be useful in identifying soft tissue abnormalities or midbrain lesions. If the clinical history suggests heavy metal or organophosphate toxicity, specialized tests, including hair or blood analysis, can be performed. Diagnostic Tests Needed The following diagnostic tests should be ordered: EMG, Tensilon test, CSF studies, and a CT scan of the head. The EMG findings in this case show potentiated muscle action potentials with rapid repetitive stimulation at 20 Hz, consistent with botulism intoxication. The Tensilon test is negative (no improvement in muscle strength with Tensilon), and the CSF protein, glucose, and cell counts are normal. The CT scan of the head reveals no meningeal enhancement or evidence of intracranial hemorrhage. Confirming the Diagnosis of Botulism To confirm botulism, serum, stool, and any leftover suspect food should be tested for the presence of botulinum toxin. The diagnostic test is a mouse bioassay. Mice are injected with dilutions of sera, stool, and food extracts, followed by injections of monovalent antitoxins (A, B, and E) and polyvalent antitoxin (ABCDE), and are observed for signs of botulism and death. Stool and food samples can also be cultured for Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that produces the toxin. To arrange testing for botulinum toxin and C. botulinum culture, the state health department should be contacted. They will provide guidance on specimen collection and storage and will forward the specimens to the state public health laboratory or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) if the state lacks testing capacity. Treatment for Botulism The cornerstone of botulism treatment is supportive care. The patient’s cardiorespiratory status should be continuously monitored in an intensive care unit. Respiratory function, as measured by forced vital capacity, should be frequently assessed, and assisted ventilation should be initiated at the first sign of respiratory decompensation. Induced vomiting or gastric lavage may be recommended to remove unabsorbed toxin from the stomach. These procedures should only be performed with a protected airway to minimize the risk of aspiration. Cathartic agents or enemas may be used to eliminate unabsorbed toxin from the gastrointestinal tract. The only pharmacological treatment for botulism is antitoxin therapy. Currently available licensed antitoxins are equine-derived antibodies targeting the toxin. One product contains antibodies against toxin types A and B, the most common causes of botulism, while another product contains antibodies against toxin types A, B, and E. The antitoxin containing antibodies to type E toxin is reserved for patients at high risk of type E botulism intoxication, such as those exposed to botulinum toxin in Alaska or those with a history of consuming preserved fish, fish eggs, seal, walrus, whale, or beaver tail. Antitoxin is most effective in preventing disease progression and shortening the duration of ventilatory failure if administered early (within 24–48 hours) after the onset of neurological symptoms. If botulism intoxication is strongly suspected, antitoxin should be administered promptly and should not be delayed until the diagnosis is confirmed. Hypersensitivity reactions to antitoxin have been reported in up to 9% of patients. Therefore, skin testing is recommended prior to antitoxin administration. Antimicrobials have not been shown to be beneficial in the treatment of foodborne botulism intoxication. Botulinum antitoxin is obtained from quarantine stations with permission for release from the CDC and some state health departments. Arrangements for antitoxin should be made through the state health department. Reporting the Case All suspected cases of botulism intoxication must be reported immediately to the local health department. The local health department will notify the state health department, which will, in turn, notify the CDC. In collaboration with state health departments, the CDC will assist with laboratory testing, arrange for treatment with botulinum antitoxin, and notify the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The FDA is responsible for investigating commercial products potentially contaminated with botulinum toxin and assessing the need for a recall. In this case, the patient denied consuming home-canned foods, suggesting that the source of botulinum toxin was a commercial product. A contaminated, widely distributed commercial product could pose a significant hazard to many individuals.
